title: Extending the Applicability of Bloom Filters by Relaxing their Parameter Constraints
summary: Standard Bloom filters constrain the number of hash functions to integers and usually constrain the bit-array length to powers of two, which can block the false-positive-optimal parameter choice. The paper proposes the Rational Bloom filter (RBF), which applies floor(k) hashes plus one deterministically activated hash with probability equal to the fractional part of k, and the Variably-Sized Block Bloom filter, which decomposes non-power-of-two lengths into power-of-two blocks. Theory proves no false negatives and RBF false positive rate no greater than a standard BF, but the experiments report unexpected local minima at integer k and no measurable insertion-time gain.

claims.statement: The Rational Bloom filter has false positive rate no greater than a standard Bloom filter with the same m and n; for the Figure 6 top setting m=8192 bits and n=1000, the target is RBF_FPR - BF_FPR <= 0.
claims.metric: difference in false positive rate (RBF minus standard BF), upper bound
claims.dataset: synthetic random elements following Figure 6 protocol
claims.config_for_value: m=8192 bits, n=1000 inserted elements, RBF k*=m/n ln2=5.678 (floor 5, activation p=0.678), standard BF same m and n with integer k=6, 10,000 non-inserted queries, MurmurHash with double hashing
claims.quote: The false positive rate pRBF FP of the RBF is smaller or equal to the false positive rate of a normal BF pBF FP

claims.statement: For m=131,072 and n=60,000, the measured RBF false-positive curve has its global minimum at k=2 and another local minimum at k=1, although the theoretical optimal k lies between them.
claims.dataset: synthetic random elements following Figure 6 protocol
claims.config_for_value: m=131072 bits, n=60000 inserted elements, k swept in [0,4], 10,000 non-inserted queries
claims.quote: has its global minimum at k = 2 and another local minimum at k = 1, although the optimal value lies in between

match_target.why: C1 is the cheapest claim that still captures the paper's central RBF result: implement an RBF and a standard BF at m=8192, n=1000 and check the inequality. The paper prints no exact FPR value for that Figure 6 top point, so the theorem's <=0 difference is the faithful target rather than a guessed numeric FPR.

tolerance.why: Rule 2: the paper reports no repeated-run std; FPR is a bounded fraction and the query set has 10,000 non-inserted elements (>=2,000), so the band is 0.01 absolute.

requirements.stmt: Represent the set with an all-zero bit array of length m; on insertion, hash each element with k pairwise independent hash functions and set the k indices to 1; on query, return absent if any index is 0, otherwise present (possible false positive).
requirements.quote: The empty filter is an all-zero bit array of length m.

requirements.stmt: For validation, compute the standard BF false-positive probability as p_FP=(1-(1-1/m)^{kn})^k, with the exponential approximation.
requirements.quote: the false positive rate pFP of the BF can be calculated [7] as

requirements.stmt: Use k* = (m/n) ln 2 as the theoretical optimal number of hash functions; at the optimum the fraction of zero bits is 1/2.
requirements.quote: For a given n, the optimal number of hash functions k∗minimize pFP with a fraction of zeros

requirements.stmt: For rational k, always apply floor(k) hash functions and add one probabilistically activated hash function whose activation probability equals the fractional part k - floor(k).
requirements.quote: In BFs the activation probability is the rational part of the number of hash functions: pactivation = k −⌊k⌋.

requirements.stmt: Make the probabilistic activation deterministic per input by deriving Hr(x) from an existing hash and activating the extra function iff Hr(x) < (k-floor(k))*m.
requirements.quote: Comparing the obtained hash value to the proportion of the maximum value p · m allows for overall probabilistic activation

requirements.stmt: Use the same deterministic activation rule for insertion and query; this preserves the no-false-negative property.
requirements.quote: As the activation is deterministic with respect to the input – due to the creation through a hash of the input

requirements.stmt: Implement the BF in C++ using MurmurHash and the Kirsch-Mitzenmacher double-hashing trick; for m=8192, compute indices with bitwise AND (m-1).
requirements.quote: we implemented the RBF and VSBBF in C++ with a Murmur Hash using the hashing trick and efficient modulo calculation with binary arithmetic

requirements.stmt: For m=8192=2^13, use hi(x) & (m-1) rather than general modulo; this is the efficient binary AND operation.
requirements.quote: It is most efficient for power-of-two filter lengths as it simplifies to a binary AND (∧) operation

requirements.stmt: Insert exactly n=1000 elements, then query 10,000 independently generated non-inserted elements and compute FPR as false positives divided by 10,000.
requirements.quote: To obtain the false positive rate, the filter was queried for 10,000 elements that had not been inserted

requirements.stmt: Compare against a standard Bloom filter with the same m, n, hash implementation, and integer k (nearest integer to k*).
requirements.quote: As a baseline, we also implemented a standard BF with the same efficiency measures.

requirements.stmt: Run the Figure 6 top configuration with filter length m=8192 bits and include n=1000 as one of the inserted-set sizes.
requirements.quote: False positive rate of a RBFs with filter sizes 8,192 (top) and 131,072 bit (bottom)

requirements.stmt: Track fraction of zeros only as a diagnostic; the grey shadow marks the near-optimal region foz=0.5±0.02, not a hard selection criterion.
requirements.quote: Experiments with a fraction of zero of 0.5±0.02 are shadowed grey.

data.name: Synthetic insertion set
data.how_to_get: Generate 1,000 uniformly random 64-bit integers with a fixed seed (e.g., 42); no external dataset is used in the paper.

data.name: Synthetic non-inserted query set
data.how_to_get: Generate 10,000 uniformly random 64-bit integers disjoint from the insertion set with a fixed seed; this matches the Figure 6 caption.
